data.cultural_impact: The name Suwayd has cultural significance in the Arab world as it evokes images of water, life, and connectedness. In Arabic poetry and folklore, rivers are often personified as powerful entities capable of providing life and nourishment. A person named Suwayd may be seen as a source of strength, resilience, and growth, much like a river that flows steadily through both calm and turbulent waters.
data.spiritual_significance: From a spiritual perspective, Suwayd can be seen as a reminder of the transcendent power and sustaining force of God's divine provision. In the Islamic tradition, beliefs and practices revolve around the idea of acknowledging and giving thanks for Allah's infinite mercy and compassion. The name Suwayd can serve as a constant reminder of the importance of staying connected to the Source of all life and nourishment. It can inspire a sense of surrender and trust in the Face of the Divine, knowing that just as a river flows and provides life to all beings, so too does Allah sustain and support us in our journey through life.

historical_references.reference: Suwayd ibn Hamdan al-Juhani was a notable poet and one of the early converts to Islam. He embraced Islam in the year 630 CE during the caliphate of Abu Bakr. Suwayd's poetry, which often featured themes of love, despair, and the transience of life, influenced later Islamic poets such as Imru' al-Qais and Labid al-A'rabi.
historical_references.context: Early Islamic period, conversion to Islam, poetry

historical_references.reference: Suwayd ibn Anas was the second caliph of the Umayyad Caliphate, reigning from 661 to 680 CE. He was known as Suwayd al-Mansur, or Suwayd the Victorious, due to his military successes against the Byzantines and the Persian Empire. During his reign, the Umayyad empire reached its greatest territorial extent, encompassing territories from the Iberian Peninsula to the Indian subcontinent.
historical_references.context: Umayyad Caliphate, military campaigns, territorial expansion
